idiom_name: immutable amount+currency value type with a currency-keyed rounding and allocation policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one immutable type holding an exact numeric amount (integer minor units plus a per-currency exponent, or an exact decimal) and a currency identity, with arithmetic closed over the type and rejecting currency mismatches. Rounding mode and scale are applied explicitly, once, at the moment money is settled, allocated or converted; splits go through an allocator that hands out the remaining minor units so the parts sum to the whole; conversion carries the rate, its timestamp and the target scale. Put the currency catalogue - exponent, symbol, cash rounding - behind the currency identity so no caller hard-codes two decimals, and keep locale formatting out of the value entirely.
code_sketch:
type Money = { amount: exact-decimal, currency: ISO4217 }

add(a, b): require a.currency == b.currency else CurrencyMismatch
round(m, mode, scale)   # explicit, once, at the boundary
allocate(m, ratios)     # largest remainder: parts always sum to m
convert(m, target, rate, mode)   # one rounding step on the target scale
format(m, locale)       # presentation only, never arithmetic
pitfalls: Skipping the explicit rounding step leaves the amount at full precision and pushes the decision into whatever consumes it.
A currency check that is a comment or a naming convention rather than an enforced precondition.
Allocation implemented as repeated division, after which the parts no longer sum to the original amount.

Wrong move: Treat JavaMoney/Moneta or any decimal library as a substitute for a currency-bearing Money value -> decimal precision does not prevent cross-currency arithmetic or a wrong minor-unit scale -> instead keep amount and currency metadata together and enforce compatible operations.

Wrong move: Convert a Money value to a float for JSON or database convenience -> binary representation can introduce cent-level drift and break reconciliation -> instead serialize integer minor units or an exact decimal string.

Wrong move: Apply a hard-coded two-decimal rule to every currency -> zero- and three-decimal currencies are rounded incorrectly -> instead read the exponent and cash-rounding policy from currency metadata.
